summary: Benin is visa-free for citizens of every African country, while all other visitors apply online for the official e-Visa (evisa.bj) before travel. Yellow fever vaccination is recommended, but vaccination cards are no longer checked at the border.

payments.text: Canada's travel advice describes a cash-based economy: credit cards are generally accepted in major hotels but rarely in restaurants and other shops, and ATMs that take foreign cards are found in banks and some large hotels but are rare outside the major cities.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office says street crime, theft and mugging are common in Cotonou and warns of carjacking in Cotonou and on roads outside towns. In the north it advises against all travel to the W and Pendjari national parks, their hunting zones and the area between Park W and the Niger border, because of terrorist attacks and kidnapping, and against all but essential travel to the rest of the Alibori and Atacora departments and to the area between the RNIE 2 highway (Tchaourou–Malanville) and the Nigerian border.

tips.text: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to the W and Pendjari national parks and nearby areas because of the risk of terrorist attacks and kidnapping, and says foreigners have been kidnapped by groups originating in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso.
Canada's travel advice warns that some fraudulent websites claim to offer Benin visas and says to use only Benin's official website (evisa.bj).

Benin's Ministry of Health has not checked vaccination cards, including the yellow fever certificate, at airports, ports or land borders since September 2026. Yellow fever vaccination remains recommended for all travellers.
Canada's travel advice says credit cards are rarely accepted beyond major hotels, and ATMs that take foreign cards are rare outside the major cities.
Canada's travel advice says most zémidjan motorcycle taxis are unregistered and are sometimes targeted by violent crime, particularly at night, and advises using only official car taxis.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Benin?
faq.answer: Citizens of all African countries enter visa-free for up to 90 days. Everyone else — including EU, UK and US passport holders — must apply online for the official e-Visa at evisa.bj before travel.

faq.question: How much does the Benin eVisa cost?
faq.answer: EUR 50 for a 30-day single-entry visa, EUR 75 for 30-day multiple entry and EUR 100 for a 90-day multiple-entry visa when you apply yourself on evisa.bj (EUR 60, 85 and 110 when applying through an embassy). The portal says processing takes from one hour to 96 hours.

faq.question: Is the yellow fever vaccine mandatory for Benin?
faq.answer: No longer at the border. Since September 2026 Benin's Ministry of Health has stopped checking vaccination cards, including yellow fever, at airports, ports and land borders. Vaccination remains recommended for all travelers, and checks can be reinstated in a public health emergency.

faq.question: Can I get a visa on arrival in Benin?
faq.answer: Canada's travel advice says you must obtain your visa before arriving in Benin, and that you can apply online through the Benin government website (evisa.bj). No official source we could read describes a visa-on-arrival scheme.

faq.question: Is Benin safe to visit?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office says street crime, including theft and mugging, is common in Cotonou. In the north it advises against all travel to the W and Pendjari national parks and nearby border areas, and against all but essential travel to the rest of the Alibori and Atacora departments and to the strip between the RNIE 2 highway and the Nigerian border.
